strengths: Integrating BORE-style optimization with label propagation and label spreading is a plausible, useful incremental contribution, particularly when a predefined candidate pool provides geometric information at little additional evaluation cost.

The empirical study covers synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-based search task. Twenty repetitions and standard errors support the reported comparisons. Figures 2 and 6 show particularly promising improvements in sample efficiency.

The equations and pseudocode make the overall construction understandable. The appendices provide substantial sensitivity analyses for kernel bandwidth, threshold ratio, unlabeled-point sampling, and pool size, including settings where additional unlabeled data does not help.
weaknesses: The central explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently supported. Sampling Gaussian neighborhoods around observations does not establish Assumption 4.1: high-density regions can cross the objective's good/bad boundary, which also changes with the threshold. Appendix C does not establish that label propagation expands the favorable decision region or improves optimization, and explicitly acknowledges that the cited classification bounds do not apply directly. A larger favorable region alone does not establish exploration under acquisition maximization.

The main contribution is not adequately isolated experimentally. Figure 12 includes a valuable control without unlabeled data, but fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the headline experiments learn beta and obtain substantially different values. The control can outperform the semi-supervised variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. Comparisons with matched or independently tuned kernel bandwidths, together with an ablation of randomized plateau selection, are needed to attribute the gains to unlabeled data.

Important comparison controls are missing. Random search is especially relevant when the budget reaches 500 evaluations from a 1,000-point synthetic pool. The manuscript also does not clearly establish whether BORE/LFBO receive the same plateau-selection heuristic or how their tree-based and discrete acquisition functions are optimized. These choices could affect the apparent exploration advantage independently of semi-supervised learning.

Evidence for broader applicability is limited. All continuous synthetic benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64D MNIST representation is trained using 440,000 separately labeled examples of the digit classes defining the optimization objective (Appendix D.5). Although the training and test data are separated, this supplies strong task-specific structure. A baseline selecting candidates directly through the pretrained classifier is needed to contextualize this experiment's value as a high-dimensional optimization benchmark.

Several reproduction-critical details remain unspecified, including input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, beta optimization bounds and initialization, and treatment of previously queried pool points. There is also a fixable mathematical inconsistency in Section 4.1: the entrywise definition of P implies column normalization, P = W D^-1, whereas the text states P = D^-1 W and Equation (7) uses P transposed. The implemented update should be made unambiguous.

The computational assessment is incomplete. Figure 8 compares subset sizes with fixed beta, but does not establish end-to-end cost relative to the baselines under the headline configuration, which learns beta repeatedly and uses 1,000 acquisition-optimization starts. Comparative timing would help determine when the reported evaluation savings justify the additional graph-processing cost.
